sacrosanct

/SAK-roh-sankt/ - the stress falls on SAK · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Sacrosanct means holy; too important to be criticized or interfered with.

The studio's master tapes were sacrosanct: engineers copied them once, then locked the originals away from every producer's 'quick fix.'

Example

Every March the botany department defends its seed vault budget as sacrosanct — heat, light, and payroll have all been cut in lean years, but no dean has ever touched the vault.

Sacrosanct began as literal law — Rome's sacrosanct officials were 'made holy' so that harming them was sacrilege — and the word still means protection raised to the level of taboo: what is sacrosanct isn't just valued, it is off-limits even to argument.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

inviolable: Inviolable marks a line that must never be crossed, protection stated as law or principle — an inviolable right, an inviolable border. Sacrosanct wraps the same protection in reverence: the thing is fenced off because it is treated as holy, so even questioning it feels like trespass.

untouchable: Untouchable states the bare outcome — no one may interfere — whatever the reason: power, fear, or law. Sacrosanct supplies a particular reason: protection carried by reverence for the thing's importance. A monopoly shielded by sheer market power is untouchable; no one calls it sacrosanct.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

negotiable: open to discussion and trade-offs

expendable: cuttable, replaceable, usable up

Where it sits · how far criticism is fenced out — respected → sacred → sacrosanct

respected vs. sacrosanct: Respected stops short of sacrosanct — what is respected gets a hearing and consideration, nothing more.

sacred vs. sacrosanct: Sacred stops short of sacrosanct — the sacred is revered, but the sacrosanct is fenced: criticism itself trespasses.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — sacro

Root — sacro: sacred (Latin sacrum)

Root — sanct

Root — sanct: made holy, made inviolable (Latin sanctus)

Put it together

Put it together: Sacro- (Latin sacrum, 'sacred') + sanct- (sanctus, 'made inviolable by rite') = holy twice over. Roman law piled the two roots together for officials whose persons were legally untouchable; English kept the double coating — sacrosanct is 'sacred' with the volume turned all the way up.

Use the root in a new word: sanctuary

Use the root in a new word: sanctuary: The wetland was declared a bird sanctuary in 1962, after a decade of stubborn petitions.

Word Choice

formal / often ironic

Sacrosanct does most of its modern work outside religion, usually with one eyebrow raised: budgets, rituals, and parking spots get called sacrosanct precisely when someone thinks the protection is excessive. For sincere reverence, say sacred; for bureaucratic untouchability, sacrosanct.
